Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then:

1. $f + g$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b (f+g) = \int_a^b f + \int_a^b g$;
2. for every real $\lambda$, $\lambda f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ and
   $\int_a^b \lambda f = \lambda \int_a^b f$;
3. consequently, for all reals $\lambda, \mu$ the function $\lambda f + \mu g$ is
   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$
4. the same identity holds with oriented limits: if $u, v \in [a,b]$ and $f, g$
   are integrable between $u$ and $v$ ([[def-oriented-integral]]), then
   $\int_u^v(\lambda f + \mu g) = \lambda\int_u^v f + \mu\int_u^v g$.

**Linearity of the integral is not linearity of the Darboux sums**, and the
proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and
$g(x) = -x$ on $[0,1]$, where the left side is $0$ and the right side is $1$ —
so $U(f+g,P)$ is in general strictly below $U(f,P) + U(g,P)$ and no identity
between upper sums is available. Claim 2, by contrast, is an identity at the
level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

derivations.claim: Regard $\mathbb C^d$ as $\mathbb R^{2d}$, so the equation in the Statement is a real first-order system to which [F1] applies. Put $z(r):=e^{-rA}y(r)$. By the product rule [F6], [F1], and [F2], $z'(r)=-Ae^{-rA}y(r)+e^{-rA}(Ay(r)+g(r,y(r)))=e^{-rA}g(r,y(r))$, since $A$ commutes with every power in the series for $e^{-rA}$.

The derivative in step 1.1 is continuous because the exponential and $g(r,y(r))$ are continuous. Thus [F3]–[F4] make it integrable componentwise, and [F5] gives $e^{-tA}y(t)-e^{-sA}y(s)=\int_s^t e^{-rA}g(r,y(r))\,dr$.

Multiply the last identity by $e^{tA}$. By [F7], this fixed linear map commutes with the componentwise integral, and [F2] gives $e^{tA}e^{-sA}=e^{(t-s)A}$ and $e^{tA}e^{-rA}=e^{(t-r)A}$. Rearranging yields the claimed formula.

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: By [F1], $U'(t)=AU(t)$. Taking conjugate transposes entrywise and using [F2], [F3], and $A^*=-A$ gives $(U(t)^*)'=U(t)^*A^*=-U(t)^*A$.
Apply the product rule [F3] to $U(t)^*U(t)$; its derivative is $-U(t)^*AU(t)+U(t)^*AU(t)=0$.

Each real and imaginary coordinate of $U(t)^*U(t)$ has zero derivative, so [F4] makes every coordinate constant. Evaluating at $t=0$ with [F1] and [F6] gives $U(t)^*U(t)=I_d$ for all $t$. By [F5] and matrix multiplication, $\|U(t)v\|_2^2=(U(t)v)^*U(t)v=v^*U(t)^*U(t)v=v^*v=\|v\|_2^2$.

Use the first-variable-linear standard inner product on $\mathbb C^n$ and its norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}|x_i|^2}$ from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]] and [[def-inner-product-norm]]. The matrix norm $\|X\|_2$ is the operator norm of the linear map $x\mapsto Xx$ in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. On $\mathbb C^0=\{0\}$ this operator norm is $0$, as specified in that definition.

For each integer $k\ge0$, define the scalar phi function and its finite-matrix action by

$$\varphi_k(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^j}{(j+k)!},\qquad \varphi_k(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^j}{(j+k)!}.$$

Here $z\in\mathbb C$, $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$, $X^0=I_n$, and factorials are the usual positive integer factorials. [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]] establishes that both series converge absolutely for every such input, so these expressions define values on their full stated domains. By the published power-series definition [[def-complex-exponential]], $\varphi_0(z)=\exp z$; for matrices, $\varphi_0(X)$ is the bounded-operator exponential series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]].

At zero, the series gives $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$ for every $n\ge0$. For $n\ge1$, only the $j=0$ matrix term can be nonzero. For $n=0$, [[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] identify $I_0$ with the unique empty matrix $0_{0\times0}$; every power $X^j$ and every partial sum is that matrix. Thus $\varphi_k(0_{0\times0})=I_0/k!=0_{0\times0}$, including $k=0$.

The recurrence is always interpreted as a series identity, including at zero; division by $z$ is not part of this definition.

For every integer $k\ge0$, the scalar series defining $\varphi_k(z)$ converges absolutely for every $z\in\mathbb C$, and the matrix series defining $\varphi_k(X)$ converges absolutely in operator $2$-norm for every $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$. At zero, $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

**operator norm** of $T$ is

above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
components and their limits are as in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]].

### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable

defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of

[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled

   integrable and
   $$\int_a^b(\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f \;+\; \mu\int_a^b g ;$$

proof of claim 1 has to squeeze rather than compute. On a subinterval the
inequality $\sup(f+g) \le \sup f + \sup g$ can be strict — take $f(x) = x$ and

level of the sums, with the roles of $\sup$ and $\inf$ exchanged when
$\lambda < 0$.

Let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge1$, $v\in\mathbb C^n$, $\beta\ge0$, $V\in M_{n\times m}(\mathbb C)$, $H\in M_m(\mathbb C)$, and $1\le m\le n$. $$e^{tA}v-u(t)=e^{tA}(v-\beta Ve_1)+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)A}(AV-VH)c(s)\,ds,$$

where the integral is oriented. Let $I_t=[0,t]$ for $t\ge0$ and $I_t=[t,0]$ for $t<0$; let $\sigma_t=1$ for $t\ge0$ and $\sigma_t=-1$ for $t<0$. If $t=0$ the integral is zero. Suppose the Arnoldi relation is

$$AV=VH+h v_{m+1}e_m^*+D+\Omega,$$

where $h\ge0$, $\|v_{m+1}\|_2=1$ when $h>0$, $D=[d_1,\ldots,d_m]$, $\eta_j\ge0$, $\|d_j\|_2\le\eta_j$, $\eta_{\rm orth}\ge0$, and $\|\Omega\|_2\le\eta_{\rm orth}$. In exact happy breakdown, interpret the rank-one term as zero and set $D=\Omega=0$. If a reduced computation returns $\widehat c(t)$ with $\|\widehat c(t)-c(t)\|_2\le\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)$ for $\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)\ge0$ and its final projection returns $\widehat x$ with $\|\widehat x-V\widehat c(t)\|_2\le\eta_{\rm proj}$ for $\eta_{\rm proj}\ge0$, then

$$\|e^{tA}v-\widehat x\|_2\le e^{|t|\mu_2(\sigma_t A)}\|v-\beta Ve_1\|_2+\int_{I_t}e^{|t-s|\mu_2(\sigma_t A)}\left(h|e_m^*c(s)|+\left(\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^m\eta_j^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)\|c(s)\|_2\right)ds+\|V\|_2\epsilon_{\rm red}(t)+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$

For exact Arnoldi from a nonzero start with no breakdown through $m$, $D=\Omega=0$, $V$ has orthonormal columns, and $v=\beta Ve_1$, recovering the standard residual integral. Whenever $AV=VH$ and $v=\beta Ve_1$, the invariant-subspace relation gives $\varphi_k(tA)v=\beta V\varphi_k(tH)e_1$ for every $k\ge0$ and every real $t$; exact happy breakdown of Arnoldi from a nonzero start is a sufficient case.

$$\epsilon_{\rm act}:=e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}+\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}\left(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^j\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth}\right)+\nu_V\epsilon_{\rm red}+\eta_{\rm proj}.$$
The stated bounds certify this expression; if any required quantity or its upward-rounded arithmetic certificate is missing, return inconclusive. For $k=0$, an action request $(0,v)$ calls [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $A$, time $h$, input $v$, index $0$, and budget $m_0$. For $k=1,2$, use the augmented-matrix construction in [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]]: let $J_k$ have ones on its superdiagonal, let $e_1,e_k$ be the first and last coordinate vectors in $\mathbb C^k$, set
$$B_k(hA,v):=\begin{bmatrix}hA&ve_1^*\\0&J_k\end{bmatrix},\qquad w_k:=\begin{bmatrix}0\\e_k\end{bmatrix},$$
and call [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]] with matrix $B_k(hA,v)$, time $1$, input $w_k$, index $0$, and budget $m_k$. By [[thm-phi-recurrence-and-augmented-matrix-actions]], the top $d$ coordinates of $e^{B_k(hA,v)}w_k$ equal $\varphi_k(hA)v$. In either case compute the full action-error bound from [[thm-arnoldi-exponential-action-error-bound]] using its certified Arnoldi relation and reduced-action data, then project to the requested vector; projection to the top coordinates cannot increase the Euclidean error. If any bound required by that theorem is missing, return inconclusive. Here $\varphi_0(hA)=e^{hA}$. Set
$$B_h:=M e^{\max(\omega,0)h};$$
the integral representations in [[lem-exponential-phi-integral-representations]] give $\|\varphi_1(hA)\|_2\le B_h$ and $\|\varphi_2(hA)\|_2\le B_h/2$.

**Outputs:** a candidate next state, a nonnegative one-step action-error bound $\delta_n$, the number of matrix-vector products, and status certified, inconclusive, or invalid-input.

**Procedure:**

1. Reject a nonpositive step, invalid dimension or budget, missing semigroup/evaluation/arithmetic bound, or nonadmissible stage with invalid-input. Evaluate $g(t,y)$ as $\widetilde q_0$ with a certified error $\eta_0$. For any zero action input, return the zero vector with action-error bound zero, as specified by the zero-start branch of [[alg-arnoldi-exponential-and-phi-actions]].
2. Request $(0,y)$ and $(1,\widetilde q_0)$ by the action routine above. If either request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. Denote their candidates by $\widehat E y$ and $\widehat P_1$ and their bounds by $\epsilon_0,\epsilon_1$.
3. For method $E$, return the candidate $\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$. If $\alpha_E$ bounds the scalar/vector arithmetic error in this combination, return
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_E.$$
4. For method $2$, first form the predictor candidate $\widetilde a=\widehat E y+h\widehat P_1$. If $\alpha_a$ bounds its arithmetic error, set $\eta_a:=\epsilon_0+h(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0)+\alpha_a$. Evaluate $g(t+h,\widetilde a)$ as $\widetilde q_a$ with a certified error $\eta_a^g$. Request $(2,\widetilde q_0)$ and $(2,\widetilde q_a)$ by the augmented-matrix action routine above; if either request is inconclusive, return inconclusive without accepting a step. With their action-error bounds $\epsilon_{20},\epsilon_{2a}$, form
$$\widetilde y^+=\widehat E y+h(\widehat P_1-\widehat P_{20}+\widehat P_{2a}),$$
where $\widehat P_{20}$ and $\widehat P_{2a}$ are the two $\varphi_2$ candidates. If $\alpha_2$ bounds the final combination arithmetic error, return
$$\delta_n=\epsilon_0+h\left(\epsilon_1+B_h\eta_0+\epsilon_{20}+\frac{B_h}{2}\eta_0+\epsilon_{2a}+\frac{B_h}{2}(L\eta_a+\eta_a^g)\right)+\alpha_2.$$
5. Return certified only when every action, field-evaluation, and arithmetic bound is finite and certified; otherwise return inconclusive and do not accept the step.

Every scalar bound computation, including the displayed $\epsilon_{\rm act}$ and $\delta_n$, is rounded upward with a certified enclosure; if its enclosure is missing or does not dominate the exact expression, return inconclusive. The direct exponential request uses at most $m_0$ products with $A$; each augmented phi request uses at most $m_k$ Arnoldi products with $B_k$, each requiring one product with $A$ plus the stated block-vector arithmetic. If all budgets are bounded by $m$, the method uses at most $2m$ products with $A$ for exponential Euler and $4m$ for ETD2, plus reduced-action and field-evaluation work. A dense implementation must report its matrix-function work and arithmetic bound through the same interface; the exact mathematical map is not a zero-cost oracle.

Let $n\ge1$ and $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$. In the standard complex inner product from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]], the adjoint matrix is the conjugate transpose $A^*$ by [[thm-matrix-of-the-adjoint-is-the-conjugate-transpose]]. The Hermitian part is $H_A:=(A+A^*)/2$. It is self-adjoint in the sense of [[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]].

Define the Euclidean logarithmic norm by $\mu_2(A):=\lambda_{\max}(H_A)$, where $\lambda_{\max}$ denotes the largest eigenvalue of the Hermitian matrix $H_A$. The item [[lem-logarithmic-norm-is-real-and-variational]] establishes that this eigenvalue exists, is real, and equals $\max_{\|x\|_2=1}\operatorname{Re}\langle Ax,x\rangle$. This is a real growth bound, not a matrix norm.

Let $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, and $t\ge0$, $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$. The inputs $y$ and all displayed stages must lie in $U$. The functions $\varphi_k(hA)$ are the finite-matrix series of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]], whose convergence is supplied by [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]].

The **exponential Euler map** is
$$\Psi^{E}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y).$$

For the two-stage **exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta map ETD2**, first form the exponential Euler predictor
$$a_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y),$$
and then set
$$\Psi^{2}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\bigl(\varphi_1(hA)-\varphi_2(hA)\bigr)g(t,y)+h\varphi_2(hA)g(t+h,a_h(t,y)).$$
These are exact mathematical step maps; an implementation must separately account for every approximate matrix-function action and arithmetic error.

For every $d\ge1$ and $X\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, the series-defined functions [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]] satisfy
$$\varphi_1(X)=\int_0^1 e^{(1-\theta)X}\,d\theta,\qquad \varphi_2(X)=\int_0^1 \theta e^{(1-\theta)X}\,d\theta.$$
The integrals are componentwise. These formulas define the values at $X=0$ directly and do not use division by $X$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

Since $\rho_B\ge\mu_2(B)$, [F9] bounds the initial term in [F2] by $e^{\rho_B\tau}\eta_{\rm init}$ and its integral by $\beta\tau e^{\tau\max(\rho_B,\rho_H)}(\gamma+\sqrt{\sum_i\eta_i^2}+\eta_{\rm orth})$. Multiplying the three phi terms by $h$, adding the certified final arithmetic error $\alpha_2$, and applying the triangle inequality gives exactly the ETD2 $\delta_n$ in [F3].

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $y$ solve $y'=Ay+g(t,y(t))$ on $[t,t+h]$, with $0<h\le T$, and put $q(r):=g(r,y(r))$. Suppose $q$ is continuously differentiable with $\sup_{t\le r\le t+h}\|q'(r)\|_2\le Q_1$, and let $K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2$. Then the exact-start local defect of the exponential Euler map satisfies
$$\|\Psi^E_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le \frac{K_+Q_1}{2}h^2.$$

Let $y'=Ay+g(t,y(t))$ on $[t,t+h]$, $0<h\le T$, and let $q(r):=g(r,y(r))$. Suppose $q\in C^2$, $\sup\|q'(r)\|_2\le Q_1$, $\sup\|q''(r)\|_2\le Q_2$, $g$ is $L$-Lipschitz in its state variable on a tube containing the exact path and predictor, and $K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2$. Set $C_E:=K_+Q_1/2$. Then the exact-start defect of $\Psi^2_h$ satisfies
$$\|\Psi^2_h(t,y(t))-y(t+h)\|_2\le K_+\left(Q_2+\frac{LC_E}{2}\right)h^3.$$

Fix $T>0$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, and define
$$K_+:=\sup_{0\le r\le T}\|e^{rA}\|_2,\qquad K_-:=\sup_{0\le r\le T}\|e^{-rA}\|_2,\qquad \kappa:=LK_+K_-.$$
These constants are finite by continuity of the finite-matrix exponential. Let $g$ be $L$-Lipschitz in its state variable on a common tube containing all states and stages below. For $0<h\le T$ and an admissible $t$, define the transformed maps
$$\Theta^E_h(t,z):=e^{-(t+h)A}\Psi^E_h(t,e^{tA}z),\qquad \Theta^2_h(t,z):=e^{-(t+h)A}\Psi^2_h(t,e^{tA}z).$$
Then
$$\|\Theta^E_h(t,z)-\Theta^E_h(t,w)\|_2\le(1+\kappa h)\|z-w\|_2,$$
and
$$\|\Theta^2_h(t,z)-\Theta^2_h(t,w)\|_2\le\left(1+h\left(\kappa+\frac{T\kappa^2}{2}\right)\right)\|z-w\|_2.$$

Suppose [[alg-certified-exponential-euler-etd2-step]] returns certified status with per-action, field-evaluation, arithmetic, and semigroup bounds as in its Definition. Let $\Psi_h^E$ or $\Psi_h^2$ be the corresponding exact map of [[def-exponential-euler-and-etd2-step-maps]], and let $\widetilde\Psi_h$ be the returned candidate map. Then the algorithm's reported value satisfies
$$\|\widetilde\Psi_h(y)-\Psi_h(y)\|_2\le\delta_n.$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, read in
the real case from [[def-norm-and-normed-space]] and in the complex case from
[[def-complex-norm-and-complex-normed-space]]. A $\mathbb K$-linear map
$T:X\to Y$ ([[def-linear-map]]) is a **bounded linear operator** when there is a
real constant $C \ge 0$ such that

$$\|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \qquad \text{for all } x \in X.$$

Any such $C$ is called a **bound** for $T$.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $X$ be a normed space over $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$ and assume
$X$ admits an ordered basis of finite length. Then $X$ is a Banach space in the
sense of [[def-banach-space]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $X$ be a real or complex normed space. If $K\subseteq X$ is nonempty compact, $C\subseteq X$ is nonempty closed, and $K\cap C=\varnothing$, then there is $\delta>0$ with
$$\|k-c\|\ge\delta\qquad(k\in K,\ c\in C).$$
No convexity, completeness, HB, or infinite choice principle is required.

Let $(X,d_X)$ and $(Y,d_Y)$ be metric spaces ([[def-metric-space]]) and let
$f : X \to Y$ be a function, with images and preimages written $f[\,\cdot\,]$
and $f^{-1}[\,\cdot\,]$ ([[def-injection-surjection-bijection]]). Conditions
(a), (b), (c), and (e) below are equivalent without choice, and each implies
(d). Assuming Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), all five are
equivalent. The authorized Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) suffices;
only its countable instance is used for the converse from (d).

- **(a)** $f$ is continuous at every point of $X$ in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$
  sense ([[def-metric-continuity]]).
- **(b)** $f^{-1}[V]$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$
  ([[def-metric-topology]]).
- **(c)** $f^{-1}[G]$ is closed in $X$ for every closed $G \subseteq Y$.
- **(d)** $f$ is **sequentially continuous**: whenever $x_k \to x$ in $(X,d_X)$,
  also $f(x_k) \to f(x)$ in $(Y,d_Y)$ ([[def-metric-convergence]]).
- **(e)** $f[\overline{A}] \subseteq \overline{f[A]}$ for every $A \subseteq X$
  ([[def-metric-interior-closure-boundary]]).

**Where choice is used.** Only the implication (d) $\Rightarrow$ (e) uses a
choice principle, and it uses it only through
[[thm-metric-sequential-closure]], whose forward direction spends the Axiom of
Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). The cycle
(a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Rightarrow$ (c) $\Rightarrow$ (e) $\Rightarrow$ (a) and
the implication (a) $\Rightarrow$ (d) are choice free.

Let $d,N,p\ge1$, $T>0$, $h=T/N$, and $t_n=nh$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb R^d$ solve an initial-value problem in an open time-state domain $D$. Use the Euclidean norm $\|v\|_2=(\sum_{i=1}^d v_i^2)^{1/2}$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]], whose triangle inequality is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]. Let $\mathcal T\subset D$ be a common compact time-state tube with positive margin in $D$, and write $\mathcal T_t:=\{v\in\mathbb R^d:(t,v)\in\mathcal T\}$. Suppose a one-step map $\Psi_{h,n}$ is defined on $\mathcal T_{t_n}$, produces $y_{n+1}=\Psi_{h,n}(y_n)$, and the entire exact path, all numerical grid states, and every method stage lie in $\mathcal T$. If constants $C,C_0,L\ge0$, independent of $N$ and $n$, satisfy
$$\|y_0-y(0)\|_2\le C_0h^p,\qquad \|\Psi_{h,n}(y(t_n))-y(t_{n+1})\|_2\le Ch^{p+1},$$
and
$$\|\Psi_{h,n}(u)-\Psi_{h,n}(v)\|_2\le(1+Lh)\|u-v\|_2$$
for every $u,v\in\mathcal T_{t_n}$ and $0\le n<N$, then, for $L>0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le\left(C_0\exp(LT)+C\frac{\exp(LT)-1}{L}\right)h^p,$$
and, for $L=0$,
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le(C_0+CT)h^p.$$

derivations.claim: Set $z(t):=e^{-tA}y(t)$. The product rule and [F1], [F6] give $z'(t)=e^{-tA}g(t,y(t))=e^{-tA}g(t,e^{tA}z(t))$, a real $2d$-dimensional ODE under [A1]. Conjugating the exact numerical map and exact endpoint by $e^{-(t+h)A}$ cancels their common $e^{hA}$ linear term and multiplies their difference by $e^{-(t+h)A}$. Hence [F2], [F3], and [F9] give transformed exact-start defects at most $K_-C_Eh^2$ and $K_-C_2h^3$.

Set $D_z:=\{(t,z):(t,e^{tA}z)\in D\}$, open as the preimage of $D$ under the continuous map $(t,z)\mapsto(t,e^{tA}z)$ by [F6], [F9], [F10], and [F12]. The map $(t,u)\mapsto(t,e^{-tA}u)$ continuously sends $\mathcal T$ to a compact tube in $D_z$ containing the transformed exact path, states, and stages; [F10]–[F11] give positive margin. Its stability is $1+L_ph$ by [F4], and its local constant is $K_-C_p$ by step 1.1. Thus [L1] applies with exact initial data.

Stability [F4], local defect [F2] or [F3] transformed by [F6] and step 1.1, and perturbation bound [F5] transformed using [F9] by $e^{-(t_{n+1})A}$ give by the triangle inequality $r_{n+1}\le(1+L_ph)r_n+K_-C_ph^{p+1}+K_-\delta_n$, with $r_0=0$.

Applying [L1] as in step 2.1 yields $\max_n\|z_n-z(t_n)\|_2\le K_-C_p\Gamma(L_p,T)h^p$. Since $y(t_n)=e^{t_nA}z(t_n)$ and [F9] with the definition of $K_+$ bounds multiplication by $e^{t_nA}$, this gives the first displayed bound.

Induction in step 2.2 gives $r_n\le K_-\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}(1+L_ph)^{n-1-j}(C_ph^{p+1}+\delta_j)$: the base case is the empty sum, and multiplying the bound for $r_n$ by $1+L_ph$ and adding the $j=n$ defect and action terms gives the formula for $r_{n+1}$.

Since $1+L_ph\le e^{L_ph}$ by [F7], each power in step 3.2 is at most $e^{L_pT}$ by [F8] and $nh\le T$. Also $Nh=T$, so $NC_ph^{p+1}=C_pT h^p$. Thus $r_n\le K_-e^{L_pT}(C_pT h^p+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_j)$. Multiplication by $e^{t_nA}$ and [F9] with the bound $K_+$ give the certified-action estimate for every $n$, hence for their maximum.

Let $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, and $t\ge0$, $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$. The inputs $y$ and all displayed stages must lie in $U$. The functions $\varphi_k(hA)$ are the finite-matrix series of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]], whose convergence is supplied by [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]].

The **exponential Euler map** is
$$\Psi^{E}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y).$$

For the two-stage **exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta map ETD2**, first form the exponential Euler predictor
$$a_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y),$$
and then set
$$\Psi^{2}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\bigl(\varphi_1(hA)-\varphi_2(hA)\bigr)g(t,y)+h\varphi_2(hA)g(t+h,a_h(t,y)).$$
These are exact mathematical step maps; an implementation must separately account for every approximate matrix-function action and arithmetic error.

Use the first-variable-linear standard inner product on $\mathbb C^n$ and its norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}|x_i|^2}$ from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]] and [[def-inner-product-norm]]. The matrix norm $\|X\|_2$ is the operator norm of the linear map $x\mapsto Xx$ in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. On $\mathbb C^0=\{0\}$ this operator norm is $0$, as specified in that definition.

For each integer $k\ge0$, define the scalar phi function and its finite-matrix action by

$$\varphi_k(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^j}{(j+k)!},\qquad \varphi_k(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^j}{(j+k)!}.$$

Here $z\in\mathbb C$, $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$, $X^0=I_n$, and factorials are the usual positive integer factorials. [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]] establishes that both series converge absolutely for every such input, so these expressions define values on their full stated domains. By the published power-series definition [[def-complex-exponential]], $\varphi_0(z)=\exp z$; for matrices, $\varphi_0(X)$ is the bounded-operator exponential series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]].

At zero, the series gives $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$ for every $n\ge0$. For $n\ge1$, only the $j=0$ matrix term can be nonzero. For $n=0$, [[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] identify $I_0$ with the unique empty matrix $0_{0\times0}$; every power $X^j$ and every partial sum is that matrix. Thus $\varphi_k(0_{0\times0})=I_0/k!=0_{0\times0}$, including $k=0$.

The recurrence is always interpreted as a series identity, including at zero; division by $z$ is not part of this definition.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

For every real $x$, $\exp(x)>0$ and
$$\exp(-x)=\frac1{\exp(x)}.$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

derivations.claim: For coordinate $i$ with $\lambda_i\in\{1,1000\}$, put $a=\lambda_i+1>0$. The exact equation is $y_i'=-ay_i+1$, $y_i(0)=0$. The product rule [F6] and chain rule [F7] show $(e^{at}y_i(t))'=e^{at}$. Integrating by [F4] gives $e^{ah}y_i(h)=\int_0^h e^{as}\,ds=(e^{ah}-1)/a$, since [F3], [F7] give antiderivative $e^{as}/a$. Dividing by the positive exponential using [F5] yields $y_i(h)=(1-e^{-ah})/a$.

By [F8], powers of $A=\operatorname{diag}(-\lambda_i)$ are diagonal with entries $(-\lambda_i)^j$, so the series [F2] evaluates the matrix phi functions coordinatewise. The exact exponential-Euler map has $e^{-\lambda_i h}y_i(0)=0$ and reaction value $g_i(0)=1$, so its coordinate is $h\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h)$. The ETD2 predictor has that same coordinate; hence $g_i(a)=1-h\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h)$ and the ETD2 coordinate is $h[(\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h)-\varphi_2(-\lambda_i h))+\varphi_2(-\lambda_i h)(1-h\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h))]=h(\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h)-h\varphi_1(-\lambda_i h)\varphi_2(-\lambda_i h))$.

In particular the stiff coordinate uses $\lambda_2h=1$: its exact, exponential-Euler, and ETD2 values are respectively $(1-e^{-1.001})/1001$, $10^{-3}\varphi_1(-1)$, and $10^{-3}(\varphi_1(-1)-10^{-3}\varphi_1(-1)\varphi_2(-1))$. All exponential and phi actions are at explicit matrix/scalar arguments; any numerical implementation must return the certificates specified by [[alg-certified-exponential-euler-etd2-step]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional inner product spaces. In orthonormal bases $\mathcal E=(e_j)$ of $V$ and $\mathcal F=(f_i)$ of $W$,

$$[T^*]_{\mathcal E\leftarrow\mathcal F}=\overline{[T]_{\mathcal F\leftarrow\mathcal E}}^{\mathsf T}.$$

Over $\mathbb R$ this is the transpose. The statement includes zero-sized bases.

Let $F$ be a field, let $m,n,p\in\mathbb N$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ and
$B=(b_{jk})\in M_{n\times p}(F)$. Their **matrix product** is the matrix
$AB\in M_{m\times p}(F)$ whose entries are

$$(AB)_{ik}:=\sum_{j\in n}a_{ij}b_{jk}.$$

The sum is the finite sum in the additive commutative monoid of $F$. If $n=0$,
it is the empty sum, so $AB$ is the zero matrix of shape $m$ by $p$.

The **identity matrix** $I_n\in M_n(F)$ has entry $1$ when $i=j$ and entry $0$
when $i\ne j$. In particular, $I_0$ is the unique empty matrix in $M_0(F)$.

For a vector $v$ in a real or complex inner product space, define its **inner-product norm** by

$$\lVert v\rVert:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}.$$

Positive definiteness in [[def-inner-product-space]] makes the radicand a nonnegative real, and [[thm-nth-roots-exist]] supplies its unique nonnegative square root. The notation therefore defines one real number $\lVert v\rVert\ge0$. Its norm axioms are established in [[cor-triangle-inequality-for-inner-product-norm]].

For $x,y\in\mathbb R^n$ and $z,w\in\mathbb C^n$, the formulas

$$\langle x,y\rangle_{\mathbb R^n}=\sum_{k<n}x_ky_k,\qquad \langle z,w\rangle_{\mathbb C^n}=\sum_{k<n}z_k\overline{w_k}$$

define inner products, linear in the first argument. At $n=0$, the unique pairing on the zero space is an inner product.

Let $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, $0\le s\le t\le T$, and let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb C^d$ be open after identifying $\mathbb C^d$ with $\mathbb R^{2d}$. Let $g:D\to\mathbb C^d$ and let $y:[s,t]\to\mathbb C^d$ be a continuously differentiable solution of the first-order system
$$y'(r)=Ay(r)+g(r,y(r)),$$
where $r\mapsto g(r,y(r))$ is continuous. With the vector integral taken componentwise after identifying $\mathbb C^d$ with $\mathbb R^{2d}$,
$$y(t)=e^{(t-s)A}y(s)+\int_s^t e^{(t-r)A}g(r,y(r))\,dr.$$

derivations.claim: Write $A=-I+N$ with $N=\begin{pmatrix}0&2e\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$; direct multiplication gives $N^2=0$ [F4]. The formula holds for $n=1$ since $A=-I+N$. If $A^n=(-1)^nI+n(-1)^{n-1}N$, multiplying by $A=-I+N$ and using $N^2=0$ gives $A^{n+1}=(-1)^{n+1}I+(n+1)(-1)^nN$, so induction proves it for every $n\ge1$. Substituting in the absolutely convergent matrix-exponential series [F2] gives $e^{tA}=e^{-t}I+\sum_{n\ge1}t^n(-1)^{n-1}N/(n-1)!=e^{-t}(I+tN)$ by the scalar series [F3].

By [F7] and step 1.1, the solution is $y(t)=e^{-t}(2et,1)^{\mathsf T}$. Direct multiplication using [F4] gives $AA^*=\begin{pmatrix}1+4e^2&-2e\\-2e&1\end{pmatrix}$ and $A^*A=\begin{pmatrix}1&-2e\\-2e&1+4e^2\end{pmatrix}$, which differ, so $A$ is nonnormal. By [F5] and [F6], its initial norm is $1$, whereas $\|y(1)\|_2=e^{-1}\sqrt{4e^2+1}>2$. For $t>0$, the exponential series gives $e^t\ge t^2/2$, and [F6] gives $e^{-t}=1/e^t\le2/t^2$; hence $e^{-t}\to0$ and $te^{-t}\le2/t\to0$, so $y(t)\to0$.

By [F1], every exact-action step is multiplication by $e^{hA}$. Repeated use of the semigroup identity in [F2] gives $(e^{hA})^n=e^{nhA}$, so the method returns $y(t_n)$ at every grid point. The transient growth is therefore present in the exact linear flow and is not removed by exponentiating this nonnormal matrix.

Use the first-variable-linear standard inner product on $\mathbb C^n$ and its norm $\|x\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{i<n}|x_i|^2}$ from [[prop-standard-coordinate-inner-products]] and [[def-inner-product-norm]]. The matrix norm $\|X\|_2$ is the operator norm of the linear map $x\mapsto Xx$ in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. On $\mathbb C^0=\{0\}$ this operator norm is $0$, as specified in that definition.

For each integer $k\ge0$, define the scalar phi function and its finite-matrix action by

$$\varphi_k(z):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^j}{(j+k)!},\qquad \varphi_k(X):=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\frac{X^j}{(j+k)!}.$$

Here $z\in\mathbb C$, $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$, $X^0=I_n$, and factorials are the usual positive integer factorials. [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]] establishes that both series converge absolutely for every such input, so these expressions define values on their full stated domains. By the published power-series definition [[def-complex-exponential]], $\varphi_0(z)=\exp z$; for matrices, $\varphi_0(X)$ is the bounded-operator exponential series of [[lem-exponential-series-of-a-bounded-operator]].

At zero, the series gives $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$ for every $n\ge0$. For $n\ge1$, only the $j=0$ matrix term can be nonzero. For $n=0$, [[def-matrix-space]] and [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]] identify $I_0$ with the unique empty matrix $0_{0\times0}$; every power $X^j$ and every partial sum is that matrix. Thus $\varphi_k(0_{0\times0})=I_0/k!=0_{0\times0}$, including $k=0$.

The recurrence is always interpreted as a series identity, including at zero; division by $z$ is not part of this definition.

For every integer $k\ge0$, the scalar series defining $\varphi_k(z)$ converges absolutely for every $z\in\mathbb C$, and the matrix series defining $\varphi_k(X)$ converges absolutely in operator $2$-norm for every $X\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, $n\ge0$. At zero, $\varphi_k(0)=1/k!$ and $\varphi_k(0_{n\times n})=I_n/k!$.

Let $d\ge1$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, $g:[0,T]\times U\to\mathbb C^d$, and $t\ge0$, $h>0$ with $t+h\le T$. The inputs $y$ and all displayed stages must lie in $U$. The functions $\varphi_k(hA)$ are the finite-matrix series of [[def-phi-functions-by-everywhere-convergent-series]], whose convergence is supplied by [[lem-phi-series-converges-absolutely]].

The **exponential Euler map** is
$$\Psi^{E}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y).$$

For the two-stage **exponential time-differencing Runge–Kutta map ETD2**, first form the exponential Euler predictor
$$a_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\varphi_1(hA)g(t,y),$$
and then set
$$\Psi^{2}_h(t,y):=e^{hA}y+h\bigl(\varphi_1(hA)-\varphi_2(hA)\bigr)g(t,y)+h\varphi_2(hA)g(t+h,a_h(t,y)).$$
These are exact mathematical step maps; an implementation must separately account for every approximate matrix-function action and arithmetic error.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$ and let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$.

1. **Fundamental theorem, second part, in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as
   a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and
   suppose $f' : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ is integrable. Then
   $$\int_a^b f' \;=\; f(b) - f(a).$$
2. **A bounded derivative gives a Lipschitz function.** Let
   $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable at
   every point of $(a,b)$, and let $M \ge 0$ satisfy
   $\lVert f'(t)\rVert_2 \le M$ for every $t \in (a,b)$. Then
   $$\lVert f(t) - f(s)\rVert_2 \;\le\; M\,|t-s| \qquad \text{for all } s,t \in [a,b],$$
   that is, $f$ is Lipschitz with constant $M$ as a map
   $([a,b], d_{\mathbb{R}}) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$
   ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]], [[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]],
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]).

Since $A=0$, $e^{hA}=1$ and $g(0,y(0))=0$. The exponential-Euler step is therefore $0+h\varphi_1(0)0=0$, and its predictor for ETD2 is also $a=0$.

At the ETD2 endpoint, $g(h,a)=h$. Its update is $0+h(\varphi_1(0)-\varphi_2(0))0+h\varphi_2(0)h=h^2/2$, which equals the exact value from step 1.1. This calculation evaluates $\varphi_k(0)$ from the series and never divides by $A$ or its eigenvalues.

Let $T>0$, $N\ge1$, $h=T/N$, $t_n=nh$, $A\in M_d(\mathbb C)$, and let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb C^d$ be open after realification, with $g:D\to\mathbb C^d$. Let $y:[0,T]\to\mathbb C^d$ solve
$$y'(t)=Ay(t)+g(t,y(t))$$
Suppose the exact path, every numerical state, and every ETD2 predictor lie in a common compact time-state tube $\mathcal T\subset D$ with positive margin. Also assume the hypotheses of [[lem-exponential-integrator-interaction-picture-stability]] hold on this tube: compared inputs in each time fiber and both associated ETD2 predictor states are admissible, and $g$ is $L_g$-Lipschitz between the states and stages used there. Finally, let $q(t):=g(t,y(t))$ be $C^2$ with $\|q'\|_2\le Q_1$ and $\|q''\|_2\le Q_2$. Assume
$$\|e^{sA}\|_2\le M e^{\omega s}\quad(0\le s\le T),\qquad M\ge1,\quad \omega\in\mathbb R,$$
and put
$$K_+:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{sA}\|_2,\quad K_-:=\sup_{0\le s\le T}\|e^{-sA}\|_2,\quad \kappa:=L_gK_+K_-.$$
These finite-matrix suprema are finite; in particular $K_+\le M e^{\max(\omega,0)T}$. Define
$$C_E:=\frac{K_+Q_1}{2},\quad C_2:=K_+\left(Q_2+\frac{L_gC_E}{2}\right),\quad L_E:=\kappa,\quad L_2:=\kappa+\frac{T\kappa^2}{2}.$$
For an exact-action exponential-Euler run use $p=1,C_p=C_E,L_p=L_E$; for exact-action ETD2 use $p=2,C_p=C_2,L_p=L_2$. If $\Gamma(L,T):=(e^{LT}-1)/L$ for $L>0$ and $\Gamma(0,T):=T$, then exact initial data give
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le K_+K_-C_p\Gamma(L_p,T)h^p.$$

Now let a certified-action implementation return candidates $\widetilde y_{n+1}$ and certified one-step action-error bounds $\delta_n$ as in [[lem-certified-exponential-step-action-error]]. Starting from $\widetilde y_0=y(0)$, its error obeys
$$\max_{0\le n\le N}\|\widetilde y_n-y(t_n)\|_2\le K_+K_-e^{L_pT}\left(C_pT h^p+\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}\delta_j\right).$$
Thus local orders one and two imply fixed-$A$, finite-dimensional global orders one and two when exact actions are used or when $\sum_j\delta_j=O(h^p)$. The constants may depend on $A$, $T$, the tube, and the derivative bounds. The bounds are not asserted uniformly over varying matrices or growing dimensions; no unbounded-operator/PDE convergence theorem follows without the additional domain and commutator hypotheses such a theorem requires.

Let $\iota_{\mathbb R}\colon\mathbb N\to\mathbb R$ be the canonical-natural map
of [[def-canonical-natural]], and let $j\colon\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ be the real
embedding $j(x)=x+i0$ from [[def-complex-numbers-and-arithmetic]]. For every
$n\in\mathbb N$, the factorial $n!$ is nonzero by
[[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], so
$\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!)>0$ by [[lem-of-naturals-positive]] and consequently
$j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))\ne0$ in the complex field
[[thm-complex-numbers-form-a-field]].

For $z\in\mathbb C$, define
$$ \exp z:=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{z^n}{j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))}. $$
whenever this complex series converges. Inside a complex expression we
abbreviate the embedded denominator $j(\iota_{\mathbb R}(n!))$ by $n!$, so the
same definition may be written $\exp z=\sum z^n/n!$ without identifying a
natural number with a complex number. Powers and series are those of
[[def-complex-integer-powers]] and
[[def-complex-series-power-series-and-absolute-convergence]]. The convergence
for every $z\in\mathbb C$ is discharged by
[[lem-complex-exponential-series-converges-everywhere]].

Let $X$ be a real or complex Banach space and let $A\in\mathcal B(X)$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). For $t\in\mathbb R$ define $E(t):=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{t^n}{n!}A^n$. Then the series converges absolutely in the operator norm $\|\cdot\|$ of $\mathcal B(X)$, uniformly for $t$ in compact subsets of $\mathbb R$; $E(t)\in\mathcal B(X)$ with $\|E(t)\| \le e^{|t|\|A\|}$; $E(0)=I$ and $E(t+s)=E(t)E(s)$ for all $s,t\in\mathbb R$; $t\mapsto E(t)$ is of class $C^\infty$ in the operator norm with $$E'(t)=AE(t)=E(t)A,$$ and $\|E(t)-I-tA\| \le\frac{t^2}{2}\|A\|^2e^{|t|\|A\|}$, so that $\frac{E(t)-I}{t}\to A$ in operator norm as $t\to0$. In particular $E$ is a uniformly continuous (hence strongly continuous) group of bounded operators on $X$ whose generator is the bounded operator $A$.
